content: Swamp Milkweed, also known as Rose Milkweed, Swamp Silkweed, or White Indian Hemp (Asclepias incarnata), is a herbaceous plant species closely related to other milkweeds. This plant thrives in moist, water-retentive to damp soils and prefers full sun to partial shade. It is commonly found growing naturally along the edges of ponds, lakes, streams, low-lying areas, or ditches. Swamp Milkweed is one of the most effective plants for attracting Monarch Butterflies. The butterflies feed on its flowers, lay their eggs on the plant, and the resulting caterpillars consume its leaves. Unlike other milkweed species, Swamp Milkweed does not produce the characteristic milky sap found in its relatives. This species has specialized roots adapted for survival in heavy, wet soils with low oxygen levels. These roots are thick, white, and scented, allowing the plant to thrive in such challenging environments. Swamp Milkweed blooms from mid to late summer, producing long, slender, rounded pods after flowering. These upright pods split open from late summer to late fall, releasing seeds attached to silky hairs. These hairs act as parachutes, enabling the seeds to be dispersed by wind currents. Swamp Milkweed is frequently cultivated, particularly in gardens designed to attract butterflies. The flowers of this plant vary in color, ranging from deep purple shades to soft pinkish-purple, with some white-flowering forms also available. Several cultivars of Swamp Milkweed exist, and the plant is often used as a fresh cut flower due to its long-lasting floral display. Additionally, its seed pods are sometimes utilized for decorative purposes.
